population.description: Danish men born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father, together with their same-gender youth community peers (neighbours in the parish of residence and schoolmates at age 15); 579,473 men with 8,683,571 earnings observations used in estimation.
population.ages: earnings observed at ages 23-49; model estimated over ages 24-45
subgroups_defined: sibling 1 (elder sibling or singleton) vs sibling 2 (younger sibling)
community defined as neighbourhood, school or both (baseline)
population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: the paper identifies variance components from the covariance structure of life-cycle earnings across persons. Family effects come from sibling covariances net of community covariances; community effects come from the difference in sibling covariances between siblings who do and do not share the youth community at age 15 (generated by family mobility between ages 11 and 15); sorting is identified from community-peer covariances.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: In the decomposition, the estimated sorting parameter sigma_FC is imputed to the family and the community factor in equal parts, so that the predicted sibling correlation is the exact sum of the family and community components (equations (10)-(11)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a convention of the decomposition; no evidence is offered for the equal split.

formal.as_written: r_S(a) = r_F(a) + r_C(a)

key_assumptions.assumption: Earnings are missing at random, so that excluding zero-earnings observations (and trimming a quarter of a percentile from each tail, and requiring at least three consecutive earnings observations) does not bias the estimated covariance structure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; the paper notes the selection rule is common in the earnings dynamics and sibling correlation literatures and is intermediate between Baker and Solon (2003) and Haider (2001). No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Community-peer moments are aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities and makes inference person-representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

threats_discussed: Transitory income shocks make current earnings a poor measure of permanent earnings (Solon, 1992; Mazumder, 2005); addressed by separating permanent from transitory components with longitudinal data.

Life-cycle bias from age differences between family members and heterogeneous earnings variation over the life cycle (Jenkins, 1987; Haider and Solon, 2006); detected in the data (Figure 2, dashed line) and controlled for in estimation.
Sorting of families into communities, which biases community influences upward unless the sorting parameter is separately identified.
Endogenous family mobility: movers and stayers may differ on unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings.
Measurement error in community affiliation from measuring the community at a single age, which would understate community effects.
Negative (boundary) variance estimates arising from unconstrained estimation.
Sparser within-cluster sampling than in comparable studies, which the paper argues reduces precision rather than introducing bias.
robustness_checks: Alternative community definitions: neighbourhood-only (column 2) and school-only (column 3) instead of the baseline (neighbourhood, school or both).
Alternative between-sibling community variation: model re-estimated on mobile families only, exploiting only the timing of family mobility (column 4).
Model estimated on immobile families only, where community effects are an upper bound (column 5).
Community-only model with community affiliation measured at ages 11 to 15 and over age intervals (Online Appendix Tables B7-B8).
Earnings percentile rank correlations instead of log earnings (Online Appendix Table B9).
Cohort shifters added to the earnings components, and estimation restricted to cohorts born 1975 or earlier (footnote 10).
Heterogeneous quadratic profiles instead of the linear HIP, and a covariance between family and community HIP slopes (footnotes 11).
Inclusion of third-born siblings (footnote 2).
Mixed-gender siblings and peers (footnote 17).
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility cannot be entirely ruled out in the absence of random assignment of families to communities.
Community effects may be understated by measurement error in community affiliation (limited exposure when community is measured at a single age).
In the immobile-family model the sorting parameter is not identified separately from community effects, so the community estimate is upward biased.

estimator.value: Equally Weighted Minimum Distance (EWMD) on the variance-covariance structure of residual log earnings

estimation.specification: Dynamic variance-components model of equations (1)-(6): permanent earnings are a heterogeneous income profile with family and community components of the intercept and slope plus an idiosyncratic random walk from age 24 (equation (2)); transitory earnings are a sibling-specific AR(1) with an exponential age spline in the innovation variance (equation (4)). Parameters are identified by matching individual, sibling (sharing / not sharing the community) and community-peer moments (equations (7)-(9)).
controls: year dummies (first-stage regression used to form residual log earnings)
quadratic age trend by three-year birth cohort group (first-stage regression)
estimation.weights: Equally weighted minimum distance; community-peer moments aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities.

heterogeneity.finding: The average community correlation of earnings is 0.023 for men and smaller, 0.012 and not significant, for women; family correlations are 0.289 for men and 0.268 for women.

heterogeneity.dimension: age (part of the life cycle over which earnings are measured)
heterogeneity.finding: Community accounts for as much as one-fifth of the sibling correlation at age 25 but becomes negligible after age 30, while family accounts for most of the correlation throughout.
Neighbourhood effects are slightly larger than school effects (men: 0.017 neighbourhood-only versus 0.008 school-only).
The community share increases somewhat when the model is estimated on mobile families only (men 0.032) or on immobile families only (men 0.038, an upper bound), but remains relatively small.

population.description: Danish women born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father, together with their same-gender youth community peers (neighbours in the parish of residence and schoolmates at age 15); 546,159 women with 8,206,022 earnings observations used in estimation.
population.ages: earnings observed at ages 23-49; model estimated over ages 24-45
subgroups_defined: sibling 1 (elder sibling or singleton) vs sibling 2 (younger sibling)
community defined as neighbourhood, school or both (baseline)
population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: the paper identifies variance components from the covariance structure of life-cycle earnings across persons. Family effects come from sibling covariances net of community covariances; community effects come from the difference in sibling covariances between siblings who do and do not share the youth community at age 15 (generated by family mobility between ages 11 and 15); sorting is identified from community-peer covariances.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: In the decomposition, the estimated sorting parameter sigma_FC is imputed to the family and the community factor in equal parts, so that the predicted sibling correlation is the exact sum of the family and community components (equations (10)-(11)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a convention of the decomposition; no evidence is offered for the equal split.

formal.as_written: r_S(a) = r_F(a) + r_C(a)

key_assumptions.assumption: Earnings are missing at random, so that excluding zero-earnings observations (and trimming a quarter of a percentile from each tail, and requiring at least three consecutive earnings observations) does not bias the estimated covariance structure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; the paper notes the selection rule is common in the earnings dynamics and sibling correlation literatures and is intermediate between Baker and Solon (2003) and Haider (2001). No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Community-peer moments are aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities and makes inference person-representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

threats_discussed: Transitory income shocks make current earnings a poor measure of permanent earnings (Solon, 1992; Mazumder, 2005); addressed by separating permanent from transitory components with longitudinal data.

Life-cycle bias from age differences between family members and heterogeneous earnings variation over the life cycle (Jenkins, 1987; Haider and Solon, 2006); detected in the data (Figure 2, dashed line) and controlled for in estimation.
Sorting of families into communities, which biases community influences upward unless the sorting parameter is separately identified.
Endogenous family mobility: movers and stayers may differ on unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings.
Measurement error in community affiliation from measuring the community at a single age, which would understate community effects.
Negative (boundary) variance estimates arising from unconstrained estimation.
Sparser within-cluster sampling than in comparable studies, which the paper argues reduces precision rather than introducing bias.
robustness_checks: Alternative community definitions: neighbourhood-only (column 2) and school-only (column 3) instead of the baseline (neighbourhood, school or both).
Alternative between-sibling community variation: model re-estimated on mobile families only, exploiting only the timing of family mobility (column 4).
Model estimated on immobile families only, where community effects are an upper bound (column 5).
Community-only model with community affiliation measured at ages 11 to 15 and over age intervals (Online Appendix Tables B7-B8).
Earnings percentile rank correlations instead of log earnings (Online Appendix Table B9).
Cohort shifters added to the earnings components, and estimation restricted to cohorts born 1975 or earlier (footnote 10).
Heterogeneous quadratic profiles instead of the linear HIP, and a covariance between family and community HIP slopes (footnotes 11).
Inclusion of third-born siblings (footnote 2).
Mixed-gender siblings and peers (footnote 17).
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility cannot be entirely ruled out in the absence of random assignment of families to communities.
Community effects may be understated by measurement error in community affiliation (limited exposure when community is measured at a single age).
In the immobile-family model the sorting parameter is not identified separately from community effects, so the community estimate is upward biased.

definition.value: Zero-mean family-specific components of the intercept (mu_f) and slope (gamma_f) of the individual-specific linear profile of the permanent component of the latent unemployment propensity; family influence is measured by the variances sigma^2_muF and sigma^2_gammaF of the Tobit-error variance components model.

timing.value: fixed over the life cycle, ages 24-40 (extrapolated to 45)

outcome.label: Initial level of the latent unemployment propensity at age 24 (intercept of the permanent unemployment profile)

register_source.value: social security records of time spent on unemployment benefits (available 1990-2009)

definition.value: Intercept of the individual-specific linear profile of the permanent component of the latent unemployment propensity (days on unemployment benefits per year, scaled 0-1,000), age measured in deviation from 24.

timing.value: age 24

units.value: variance of the family component of the age-24 intercept of the latent unemployment propensity (squared units of days on benefits per year, scaled 0-1,000)

estimand.target_population: Danish women born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father (sibling pairs and their same-gender youth community peers)
estimand.time_horizon: initial unemployment at age 24
estimand.formal_query: Parameter of the estimated variance-components model: (A) Shared components (heterogeneous profile-random growth), Family (sigma^2_muF), Variance of intercepts

population.description: Danish women born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father, together with their youth community peers, excluding the two youngest cohort groups (1981 and 1984); 546,159 women (8,206,022 earnings observations in the earnings analysis).
population.birth_cohorts: 1965-85 excluding the two youngest cohort groups (1981 and 1984)
population.ages: unemployment observed from age 23; model estimated over ages 24-40 and extrapolated to 45
subgroups_defined: sibling 1 (elder sibling or singleton) vs sibling 2 (younger sibling)
community defined as neighbourhood, school or both (baseline)
population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: variance components of the latent unemployment propensity are identified from the covariance structure of Tobit errors across time, siblings (sharing and not sharing the community) and community peers.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the modelling device that handles the mass of zeros (81% of male and 73% of female observations); right-censoring at 1,000 is reported to be negligible (0.02% and 0.03%).

formal.as_written: l_ifca = w*_ifca x I(w*_ifca > 0); w*_ifca = beta_bt(0) + beta_bt(1) a + beta_bt(2) a^2 + w_ifca

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Community-peer moments are aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities and makes inference person-representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

threats_discussed: The large mass of zeros (81% of men, 73% of women) makes a linear variance-components model inappropriate; handled by the Tobit formulation.
Right-censoring at 1,000 days, reported as negligible (0.02% of men, 0.03% of women).
Only a diagonal fourth-moments matrix is available for inference, because individual-level deviations of the latent process are not observed.
Convergence problems of the EWMD estimator, addressed by weighting Minimum Distance with the inverse fourth-moments matrix.
Unemployment benefit data end in 2009, so the two youngest cohort groups are dropped and the 41-5 age range is extrapolated.
Sorting of families into communities.
robustness_checks: Comparison of the life-cycle profile of the decomposition with the earnings results (Figure 10).
Life-cycle averages computed over ages 24-45 from parameters estimated on the 24-40 span.
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility (shared with the earnings analysis): no random assignment of families to communities.
Only the variance of each estimated moment, not the cross-moment covariances, can be retrieved, so inference uses a diagonal fourth-moments matrix.

estimator.value: Minimum Distance on the covariance structure of Tobit errors, weighted by the inverse diagonal fourth-moments matrix (Tobit dynamic variance-components model)

estimation.specification: Tobit version of the dynamic variance-components model: observed days on unemployment benefits are a censored realisation of a latent linear propensity (equation (13)) that depends on a period- and cohort-specific quadratic polynomial in age plus the composite error of equation (1) (equation (14)). Empirical covariances of the latent process are recovered as error covariances of single- and two-equation Tobit systems and matched to the moments implied by the model of Section 3.
controls: period- and cohort-specific intercept of the latent propensity
period- and cohort-specific linear age term
period- and cohort-specific quadratic age term
estimation.weights: Minimum Distance weighted by the inverse of a diagonal fourth-moments matrix (to overcome convergence problems of EWMD); peer covariances estimated with a maximum likelihood estimator weighted by the Page and Solon (2003a) scheme.

sample_n.value: 546,159 women; 6,830 empirical variances and covariances used in estimation

heterogeneity.finding: For men communities affect initial unemployment but not life-cycle dynamics, and the family intercept-slope covariance is positive (state dependence); for women the family intercept-slope covariance is negative, consistent with the human capital interpretation.
For both genders family is by far the most relevant shared factor of unemployment dynamics.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).

population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: variance components of the latent unemployment propensity are identified from the covariance structure of Tobit errors across time, siblings (sharing and not sharing the community) and community peers.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the modelling device that handles the mass of zeros (81% of male and 73% of female observations); right-censoring at 1,000 is reported to be negligible (0.02% and 0.03%).

formal.as_written: l_ifca = w*_ifca x I(w*_ifca > 0); w*_ifca = beta_bt(0) + beta_bt(1) a + beta_bt(2) a^2 + w_ifca

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: In the decomposition, the estimated sorting parameter sigma_FC is imputed to the family and the community factor in equal parts, so that the predicted sibling correlation is the exact sum of the family and community components (equations (10)-(11)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a convention of the decomposition; no evidence is offered for the equal split.

formal.as_written: r_S(a) = r_F(a) + r_C(a)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: variance components of the latent unemployment propensity are identified from the covariance structure of Tobit errors across time, siblings (sharing and not sharing the community) and community peers.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the modelling device that handles the mass of zeros (81% of male and 73% of female observations); right-censoring at 1,000 is reported to be negligible (0.02% and 0.03%).

formal.as_written: l_ifca = w*_ifca x I(w*_ifca > 0); w*_ifca = beta_bt(0) + beta_bt(1) a + beta_bt(2) a^2 + w_ifca

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: In the decomposition, the estimated sorting parameter sigma_FC is imputed to the family and the community factor in equal parts, so that the predicted sibling correlation is the exact sum of the family and community components (equations (10)-(11)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a convention of the decomposition; no evidence is offered for the equal split.

formal.as_written: r_S(a) = r_F(a) + r_C(a)

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Community-peer moments are aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities and makes inference person-representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

threats_discussed: The large mass of zeros (81% of men, 73% of women) makes a linear variance-components model inappropriate; handled by the Tobit formulation.
Right-censoring at 1,000 days, reported as negligible (0.02% of men, 0.03% of women).
Only a diagonal fourth-moments matrix is available for inference, because individual-level deviations of the latent process are not observed.
Convergence problems of the EWMD estimator, addressed by weighting Minimum Distance with the inverse fourth-moments matrix.
Unemployment benefit data end in 2009, so the two youngest cohort groups are dropped and the 41-5 age range is extrapolated.
Sorting of families into communities.

Life-cycle averages computed over ages 24-45 from parameters estimated on the 24-40 span.

Empirical covariances of the latent process are recovered as error covariances of single- and two-equation Tobit systems and matched to the moments implied by the model of Section 3.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: the paper identifies variance components from the covariance structure of life-cycle earnings across persons. Family effects come from sibling covariances net of community covariances; community effects come from the difference in sibling covariances between siblings who do and do not share the youth community at age 15 (generated by family mobility between ages 11 and 15); sorting is identified from community-peer covariances.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Earnings are missing at random, so that excluding zero-earnings observations (and trimming a quarter of a percentile from each tail, and requiring at least three consecutive earnings observations) does not bias the estimated covariance structure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; the paper notes the selection rule is common in the earnings dynamics and sibling correlation literatures and is intermediate between Baker and Solon (2003) and Haider (2001). No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Cohort effects in mean earnings are integrated out by the first-stage regressions (year dummies and a quadratic age trend by three-year birth cohort group), so the dynamics model needs no cohort shifters.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 10: robustness checks that included cohort shifters on the earnings components produced results entirely in line with the baseline, and estimating the model only on cohorts born 1975 or earlier did not change the substance of the findings.

threats_discussed: Transitory income shocks make current earnings a poor measure of permanent earnings (Solon, 1992; Mazumder, 2005); addressed by separating permanent from transitory components with longitudinal data.

Life-cycle bias from age differences between family members and heterogeneous earnings variation over the life cycle (Jenkins, 1987; Haider and Solon, 2006); detected in the data (Figure 2, dashed line) and controlled for in estimation.
Sorting of families into communities, which biases community influences upward unless the sorting parameter is separately identified.
Endogenous family mobility: movers and stayers may differ on unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings.
Measurement error in community affiliation from measuring the community at a single age, which would understate community effects.
Negative (boundary) variance estimates arising from unconstrained estimation.
Sparser within-cluster sampling than in comparable studies, which the paper argues reduces precision rather than introducing bias.
robustness_checks: Alternative community definitions: neighbourhood-only (column 2) and school-only (column 3) instead of the baseline (neighbourhood, school or both).
Alternative between-sibling community variation: model re-estimated on mobile families only, exploiting only the timing of family mobility (column 4).
Model estimated on immobile families only, where community effects are an upper bound (column 5).
Community-only model with community affiliation measured at ages 11 to 15 and over age intervals (Online Appendix Tables B7-B8).
Earnings percentile rank correlations instead of log earnings (Online Appendix Table B9).
Cohort shifters added to the earnings components, and estimation restricted to cohorts born 1975 or earlier (footnote 10).
Heterogeneous quadratic profiles instead of the linear HIP, and a covariance between family and community HIP slopes (footnotes 11).
Inclusion of third-born siblings (footnote 2).
Mixed-gender siblings and peers (footnote 17).
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility cannot be entirely ruled out in the absence of random assignment of families to communities.
Community effects may be understated by measurement error in community affiliation (limited exposure when community is measured at a single age).
In the immobile-family model the sorting parameter is not identified separately from community effects, so the community estimate is upward biased.

population.description: Danish men born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father, together with their same-gender youth community peers (neighbours in the parish of residence and schoolmates at age 15); 579,473 men with 8,683,571 earnings observations used in estimation.
population.ages: earnings observed at ages 23-49; model estimated over ages 24-45
subgroups_defined: sibling 1 (elder sibling or singleton) vs sibling 2 (younger sibling)
community defined as neighbourhood, school or both (baseline)
population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: the paper identifies variance components from the covariance structure of life-cycle earnings across persons. Family effects come from sibling covariances net of community covariances; community effects come from the difference in sibling covariances between siblings who do and do not share the youth community at age 15 (generated by family mobility between ages 11 and 15); sorting is identified from community-peer covariances.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Earnings are missing at random, so that excluding zero-earnings observations (and trimming a quarter of a percentile from each tail, and requiring at least three consecutive earnings observations) does not bias the estimated covariance structure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; the paper notes the selection rule is common in the earnings dynamics and sibling correlation literatures and is intermediate between Baker and Solon (2003) and Haider (2001). No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Cohort effects in mean earnings are integrated out by the first-stage regressions (year dummies and a quadratic age trend by three-year birth cohort group), so the dynamics model needs no cohort shifters.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 10: robustness checks that included cohort shifters on the earnings components produced results entirely in line with the baseline, and estimating the model only on cohorts born 1975 or earlier did not change the substance of the findings.

threats_discussed: Transitory income shocks make current earnings a poor measure of permanent earnings (Solon, 1992; Mazumder, 2005); addressed by separating permanent from transitory components with longitudinal data.

Life-cycle bias from age differences between family members and heterogeneous earnings variation over the life cycle (Jenkins, 1987; Haider and Solon, 2006); detected in the data (Figure 2, dashed line) and controlled for in estimation.
Sorting of families into communities, which biases community influences upward unless the sorting parameter is separately identified.
Endogenous family mobility: movers and stayers may differ on unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings.
Measurement error in community affiliation from measuring the community at a single age, which would understate community effects.
Negative (boundary) variance estimates arising from unconstrained estimation.
Sparser within-cluster sampling than in comparable studies, which the paper argues reduces precision rather than introducing bias.
robustness_checks: Alternative community definitions: neighbourhood-only (column 2) and school-only (column 3) instead of the baseline (neighbourhood, school or both).
Alternative between-sibling community variation: model re-estimated on mobile families only, exploiting only the timing of family mobility (column 4).
Model estimated on immobile families only, where community effects are an upper bound (column 5).
Community-only model with community affiliation measured at ages 11 to 15 and over age intervals (Online Appendix Tables B7-B8).
Earnings percentile rank correlations instead of log earnings (Online Appendix Table B9).
Cohort shifters added to the earnings components, and estimation restricted to cohorts born 1975 or earlier (footnote 10).
Heterogeneous quadratic profiles instead of the linear HIP, and a covariance between family and community HIP slopes (footnotes 11).
Inclusion of third-born siblings (footnote 2).
Mixed-gender siblings and peers (footnote 17).
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility cannot be entirely ruled out in the absence of random assignment of families to communities.
Community effects may be understated by measurement error in community affiliation (limited exposure when community is measured at a single age).
In the immobile-family model the sorting parameter is not identified separately from community effects, so the community estimate is upward biased.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 10: robustness checks that included cohort shifters on the earnings components produced results entirely in line with the baseline, and estimating the model only on cohorts born 1975 or earlier did not change the substance of the findings.

threats_discussed: Transitory income shocks make current earnings a poor measure of permanent earnings (Solon, 1992; Mazumder, 2005); addressed by separating permanent from transitory components with longitudinal data.

Life-cycle bias from age differences between family members and heterogeneous earnings variation over the life cycle (Jenkins, 1987; Haider and Solon, 2006); detected in the data (Figure 2, dashed line) and controlled for in estimation.
Sorting of families into communities, which biases community influences upward unless the sorting parameter is separately identified.
Endogenous family mobility: movers and stayers may differ on unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings.
Measurement error in community affiliation from measuring the community at a single age, which would understate community effects.
Negative (boundary) variance estimates arising from unconstrained estimation.
Sparser within-cluster sampling than in comparable studies, which the paper argues reduces precision rather than introducing bias.
robustness_checks: Alternative community definitions: neighbourhood-only (column 2) and school-only (column 3) instead of the baseline (neighbourhood, school or both).
Alternative between-sibling community variation: model re-estimated on mobile families only, exploiting only the timing of family mobility (column 4).
Model estimated on immobile families only, where community effects are an upper bound (column 5).
Community-only model with community affiliation measured at ages 11 to 15 and over age intervals (Online Appendix Tables B7-B8).
Earnings percentile rank correlations instead of log earnings (Online Appendix Table B9).
Cohort shifters added to the earnings components, and estimation restricted to cohorts born 1975 or earlier (footnote 10).
Heterogeneous quadratic profiles instead of the linear HIP, and a covariance between family and community HIP slopes (footnotes 11).
Inclusion of third-born siblings (footnote 2).
Mixed-gender siblings and peers (footnote 17).
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility cannot be entirely ruled out in the absence of random assignment of families to communities.
Community effects may be understated by measurement error in community affiliation (limited exposure when community is measured at a single age).
In the immobile-family model the sorting parameter is not identified separately from community effects, so the community estimate is upward biased.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the modelling device that handles the mass of zeros (81% of male and 73% of female observations); right-censoring at 1,000 is reported to be negligible (0.02% and 0.03%).

key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

population.description: Danish women born 1965-85 who are the first or second child of a sampled father, together with their youth community peers, excluding the two youngest cohort groups (1981 and 1984); 546,159 women (8,206,022 earnings observations in the earnings analysis).
population.birth_cohorts: 1965-85 excluding the two youngest cohort groups (1981 and 1984)
population.ages: unemployment observed from age 23; model estimated over ages 24-40 and extrapolated to 45
subgroups_defined: sibling 1 (elder sibling or singleton) vs sibling 2 (younger sibling)
community defined as neighbourhood, school or both (baseline)
population.selection: First and second children of sampled fathers born 1965-85 who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; excluding children also observed as parents of children born 1965-85, siblings born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart, and pupils in schools exclusively for special educational needs; earnings observations must be non-zero, are trimmed by a quarter of a percentile in each tail, and an individual must have at least three consecutive earnings observations; community peers are added irrespective of birth order and spacing.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous shock or reform: variance components of the latent unemployment propensity are identified from the covariance structure of Tobit errors across time, siblings (sharing and not sharing the community) and community peers.

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed days on unemployment benefits are generated by an underlying latent linear unemployment propensity through a Tobit mapping, and all components of the composite error are zero-mean normally distributed with the second moments of equations (1)-(6).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the modelling device that handles the mass of zeros (81% of male and 73% of female observations); right-censoring at 1,000 is reported to be negligible (0.02% and 0.03%).

formal.as_written: l_ifca = w*_ifca x I(w*_ifca > 0); w*_ifca = beta_bt(0) + beta_bt(1) a + beta_bt(2) a^2 + w_ifca

key_assumptions.assumption: Residual log earnings are the sum of a permanent and a transitory component which are orthogonal by construction: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0 (equation (1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a definitional restriction; the paper notes it implies that the moment restrictions of the full model are the sum of the permanent and transitory moment restrictions.

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca v_ifca) = 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The shared and idiosyncratic components are zero-mean random variables with the second-moment structure imposed in assumptions (3.a)-(3.d): family and community intercepts and slopes have unrestricted within-factor covariances, the idiosyncratic permanent shock is a random walk from age 24, and the only cross-factor dependence is cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Set out explicitly in equations (3.a)-(3.d); footnote 11 reports that allowing in addition a covariance between the family and community HIP slopes gave a positive, non-significant estimate and virtually unaffected remaining parameters.

formal.as_written: (mu_f, gamma_f) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muF, sigma^2_gammaF, sigma_mu-gamma-F); (mu_c, gamma_c) ~ (0, 0; sigma^2_muC, sigma^2_gammaC, sigma_mu-gamma-C); cov(mu_f, mu_c) = sigma_FC

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle profiles of the shared permanent components are linear in age (a linear heterogeneous income profile).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 reports that a more general model with heterogeneous quadratic profiles yields results very similar to the linear HIP; the linear form is kept for simplicity and ease of interpretation.

formal.as_written: pi_t[(mu_f + mu_c) + (gamma_f + gamma_c) a + omega_ia]

key_assumptions.assumption: Community peers from different families share no family-specific component: the covariance of permanent earnings between peers depends only on community and sorting effects, not on family effects (equation (9)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the moment restrictions of equation (9); it is what allows family effects to be identified net of community influences by combining equations (8) and (9).

formal.as_written: E(y_ifca, y_i'f'ca') = [sigma^2_muC + sigma^2_gammaC a a' + sigma_mu-gamma-C (a + a') + 2 sigma_FC]

key_assumptions.assumption: Families who move between the ages at which the two siblings are exposed to the community are comparable to immobile families, so that between-sibling community variation generated by family mobility identifies community effects separately from sorting.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the assumption the identification of the sorting parameter rests on; the paper concedes the two types of family may differ on unobservables that also affect earnings, and re-estimates the model on mobile families only (exploiting only the timing of mobility) as a check.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sample is conditioned on being the first or second child of a sampled father, sharing both legal parents from registration at birth, not adopted, not themselves a parent of a child born 1965-85, and born between 12 months and 12 years apart; peers are selected irrespective of birth order and spacing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection rules are listed in Subsection 1.1; footnote 2 reports that including third-born siblings produced results entirely consistent with those presented.

implies_edges.from: sibling-pair sample selection (first two children, 12 months to 12 years apart)

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is correctly specified, so that the theoretical moments implied by the model equal their empirical counterparts (individual, sibling and community-peer variances and covariances), which is what Minimum Distance estimation matches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Identification is described as resting on three sets of moment restrictions; the paper reports no over-identification test of the moment conditions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Community-peer moments are aggregated across communities with the weighting scheme of Page and Solon (2003a), which gives greater importance to more populous communities and makes inference person-representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2 and Subsection 3.5; no alternative weighting is reported.

threats_discussed: The large mass of zeros (81% of men, 73% of women) makes a linear variance-components model inappropriate; handled by the Tobit formulation.
Right-censoring at 1,000 days, reported as negligible (0.02% of men, 0.03% of women).
Only a diagonal fourth-moments matrix is available for inference, because individual-level deviations of the latent process are not observed.
Convergence problems of the EWMD estimator, addressed by weighting Minimum Distance with the inverse fourth-moments matrix.
Unemployment benefit data end in 2009, so the two youngest cohort groups are dropped and the 41-5 age range is extrapolated.
Sorting of families into communities.
robustness_checks: Comparison of the life-cycle profile of the decomposition with the earnings results (Figure 10).
Life-cycle averages computed over ages 24-45 from parameters estimated on the 24-40 span.
unresolved_confounders: Bias due to endogenous family mobility (shared with the earnings analysis): no random assignment of families to communities.
Only the variance of each estimated moment, not the cross-moment covariances, can be retrieved, so inference uses a diagonal fourth-moments matrix.

Empirical covariances of the latent process are recovered as error covariances of single- and two-equation Tobit systems and matched to the moments implied by the model of Section 3.
controls: period- and cohort-specific intercept of the latent propensity
period- and cohort-specific linear age term
period- and cohort-specific quadratic age term
estimation.weights: Minimum Distance weighted by the inverse of a diagonal fourth-moments matrix (to overcome convergence problems of EWMD); peer covariances estimated with a maximum likelihood estimator weighted by the Page and Solon (2003a) scheme.
